content: Ammonium sulfate, chemically represented as (NH₄)₂SO₄, is an inorganic compound widely utilized as a fertilizer. It contains 21% nitrogen in the form of ammonium ions and 24% sulfur in the form of sulfate ions. Ammonium sulfate is insoluble in alcohol and liquid ammonia. It exhibits slight hygroscopic properties, meaning it can absorb moisture from the air when the relative humidity exceeds 81% at approximately 20°C. Commercially, ammonium sulfate is synthesized by reacting ammonia with sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). It can also be produced from the ammoniacal liquor of gas works and subsequently purified through recrystallization. The compound forms large rhombic prisms, has a mildly saline taste, and is highly soluble in water. When its aqueous solution is boiled, some ammonia is lost, resulting in the formation of an acidic sulfate. Ammonium sulfate is extensively used as an artificial fertilizer, particularly for alkaline soils. In the soil, the sulfate ion is released and reacts to form sulfuric acid, which lowers the soil's pH while simultaneously providing essential nitrogen to support plant growth. Additionally, it serves as an agricultural spray adjuvant for water-soluble insecticides, herbicides, and fungicides. In this role, it binds iron and calcium cations present in well water and plant cells, enhancing the efficacy of these chemicals. It is especially effective as an adjuvant for herbicides such as 2,4-D (amine), glyphosate, and glufosinate. Ammonium sulfate is also employed in the preparation of other ammonium salts. In biochemistry, it is commonly used for protein purification through ammonium sulfate precipitation. Furthermore, it is listed as an ingredient in several vaccines in the United States, as per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Lastly, ammonium sulfate is utilized as a food additive.
